A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BBQ-derived visual stereotype benchmark, renamed from SB-Bench to BBQ-V. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison. The redesigned dataset and scoring protocol prevent direct comparison of many performance values, but do not limit document comparability.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of nine LMMs, model-scaling experiments, modality comparisons, and option/image-shuffling analyses in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of 19 LMMs, disambiguated and synthetic-image experiments, human–judge agreement, and comparisons between automated judges.

M1.justification: The benchmark-construction procedure changes substantially. v1 uses Qwen-2.5 querying/anonymization, CLIP filtering, and a dual-query stitching procedure. v3 describes GPT-4o-mini querying/anonymization, OCR filtering, agreement among three semantic-alignment models, synthetic/leakage screening, and face blurring (Section 3.1; Appendices L–O). These are procedural changes, beyond renaming or additional documentation.

E1.justification: The nine broad domains remain, but represented subgroups change from 60 to 50. Disability coverage, for example, contracts from eight groups including autism and mental illness to physical disability and blindness (v1 Figure A.2; v3 Figure A.1). v3 also evaluates disambiguated contexts and synthetic-image counterparts, adding materially different evidence conditions and visual environments.

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from nine to 19 models. Additions include InternVL3, Gemma-3, Aya-Vision, Qwen2.5 variants, Phi-4, and three thinking models; Gemini-1.5-Flash is replaced by Gemini-2.0-Flash and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite. Scaling comparisons also switch to InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL and omit the earlier LLaVA scaling comparison.

E3.justification: v1 primarily evaluates 7,500 MCQs using answer correctness and bias rates. v3 reports 14,144 question–image pairs over 4,497 real images, primarily using open-ended rationales and answers scored by GPT-4.1-mini on five ordinal criteria, with harmonic-mean summaries. New disambiguated controls use spatial references and accuracy/grounding criteria; synthetic experiments compare matched real-image subsets. These are substantial replacements and additions to evaluation design.

E4.justification: Blind-versus-vision, base-LLM, and scaling analyses already exist in v1 and are revised in v3. v3 adds disambiguated controls, real-versus-synthetic sensitivity tests, criterion-level error analyses, thinking-model case studies, and human/alternative-judge validation. Conversely, v1's option/image-shuffling tests and MCQ–reasoning correlation analysis are not retained as corresponding analyses.

E5.justification: Statistical validation shifts from v1's shuffle standard deviations and MCQ–reasoning correlation to human–judge agreement statistics in v3. Appendix V and Table A.5 introduce observed agreement and Cohen's kappa, including quadratic weighting, for 1,000 sampled responses; overall agreement is 0.9100 and weighted kappa 0.8128. This does not establish any increase in repeated or seeded benchmark runs.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded. In v1 Table 3, GPT-4o leads with 10.79% bias, and InternVL2-8B is the best listed open model at 62.00%. In v3 Table 3, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite leads at 80.89%, and Phi-4-MM leads the listed open models at 74.30%. These use different data and scoring, so they are not direct performance gains. Disambiguated, synthetic-image, and judge-validation results are newly reported.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. v3's ordinal scoring rubrics, harmonic-mean reporting, and agreement statistics change empirical evaluation rather than introduce a theoretical contribution.

C1.justification: The contribution shifts from a comprehensive MCQ benchmark to a rationale-sensitive, open-ended benchmark. v3's abstract adds the claim that thinking models induce more bias in reasoning chains, while its conclusion adds claims about synthetic-image distribution shifts and advantages over multiple-choice evaluation. These materially expand and redefine the central claims.

C2.justification: v1 treats agreement between MCQ answers and reasoning as evidence of benchmark robustness. v3 instead argues that constrained choices can inflate scores, interprets ambiguity handling as a principal failure mechanism, and attributes additional failures to reasoning chains and synthetic visual cues. Appendix A newly identifies missing intersectional evaluation and explicitly excludes bias mitigation; the earlier warning about internet-image bias remains.

D1.justification: v1 provides model architectures and prompt templates but relatively limited execution settings. v3 adds detailed scoring rubrics, filtering prompts and thresholds, hardware/software information, and inference settings including temperature 0, 1,024 maximum tokens, resolution 512, batch size 256, and bfloat16. Synthetic-generation settings are also documented. Newly disclosed settings do not, by themselves, establish changes to earlier experiments.

R1.justification: The comparative positioning changes substantively: v1 promotes MCQs as easier to evaluate than open-ended benchmarks, whereas v3 emphasizes open-ended reasoning and real multi-actor scenes over MCQ and synthetic alternatives. v3 adds VLBiasBench to the benchmark comparison and cites newer reasoning models and synthetic–authentic domain-gap research. Much of the underlying related-work survey remains.

P1.justification: Beyond the benchmark/title rename, the abstract, introduction, construction description, evaluation narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v3 introduces a dedicated discussion subsection and reorganizes the appendix around controls, scoring criteria, filtering, computation, and validation. Ethical limitations and social impact move from the main text into the supplement.

P2.justification: v3 moves the taxonomy graphic to the opening page, redraws the construction pipeline, and removes the separate paired-image pipeline figure. Comparison tables are expanded, example panels are redesigned, and new radar plots, a synthetic–real heatmap, agreement tables, and structured prompt boxes substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens measurement validation and reproducibility: disambiguated controls address whether failures reflect missing evidence, human and alternative-judge comparisons assess evaluator reliability, and detailed rubrics/settings make the procedure more inspectable (Appendices E, Q, and V). These address important weaknesses of v1's primarily MCQ-based validation. Disability coverage narrows, and some interpretations remain overstated, particularly causal claims about thinking from unmatched model comparisons. Nevertheless, the added controls and documented validation provide a substantial net improvement.
